triage.name: Allergic contact dermatitis
triage.reason: Pruritic eczematous rash with a clear exposure history and distribution; diagnosed by pattern recognition and patch testing.

review_issues: auto-repaired: workup: 'cbc' was in supporting, not_indicated; kept supporting as a conditional order (only if systemic symptoms, extensive rash or concern for infection)
auto-repaired: workup: 'skin_culture' was in supporting, not_indicated; kept supporting as a conditional order (only if secondary bacterial infection is suspected)
presentation: term 'Localized skin rash' not found in SNOMED CT
exam: term 'Demarcated skin lesion' not found in SNOMED CT

demographics: More common in adults than children, reflecting cumulative lifetime exposure to allergens
Occupational exposures account for a substantial share of cases in working-age adults
Nickel allergy is more common in women, often related to jewelry and ear piercing

risk_factors.text: Occupational skin exposure to allergens (hairdressing, healthcare, cleaning, metalworking, construction)
Personal history of atopic dermatitis or other atopic disease
Ear piercing or regular use of nickel-containing jewelry
Repeated use of topical products containing fragrance, preservatives or antibiotics
Outdoor exposure to poison ivy, oak or sumac
Female sex for nickel and cosmetic-related allergy

social_history: Hobbies or work involving plants, solvents, dyes, cement or adhesives
Frequent hand washing or wet work
exposures: Poison ivy, oak or sumac sap
Fragrances and preservatives in cosmetics, soaps and lotions
Topical antibiotics such as neomycin or bacitracin
Rubber accelerators in gloves and shoes
Hair dyes, permanent wave solutions and other salon chemicals
Cement, epoxy resins and industrial adhesives
Airborne allergens such as plant sap soot from burning vegetation

chief_complaints.text: The rash is in the same spot where I came into contact with something
It started as red bumps and now it is blistering and oozing

hpi.onset: Gradual, typically 24–72 hours after re-exposure in a sensitized person; up to 7–21 days after first-ever exposure
hpi.duration: Days to weeks if exposure continues; improves within 1–3 weeks after the allergen is removed
hpi.progression: Begins as redness and itching, then develops papules and vesicles that may weep and crust; spreads to areas touched by contaminated hands or clothing
hpi.location: Confined to skin that contacted the allergen; common sites are the hands, forearms, face, neck, earlobes, wrists, waistband and feet
hpi.quality: Intensely itchy, burning or stinging; skin feels raw and tender
hpi.severity: Mild to severe; itching is often the most bothersome feature and can interfere with sleep
hpi.timing: Continuous while exposure continues; itching is often worse at night

associated_symptoms.text: Oozing and crusting of the rash
Darkening of the skin where the rash healed

pertinent_negatives: Rash spreading to skin that never touched the allergen
Recent new medication taken by mouth
Sick contacts with a similar rash
History of psoriasis or lichen planus

argues_against: Pustules or honey-colored crust suggesting bacterial infection
Well-demarcated plaques with silvery scale suggesting psoriasis
Violaceous flat-topped papules suggesting lichen planus

positives.text: Known sensitivity to a contact allergen

argues_against: Rapid generalized urticaria or anaphylaxis suggesting immediate hypersensitivity
Fever or systemic illness suggesting infection or systemic disease
Airborne allergen causing respiratory symptoms rather than isolated skin disease

atypical.how_it_differs: More often affects the face, hands and diaper area; the child may be irritable and scratch constantly, and the history of exposure may be unclear.
The rash may be drier and less blistering, and is more often caused by topical medications or dressings; itching can be severe with minimal visible inflammation.
The rash may be mistaken for a pregnancy-specific dermatosis; management focuses on avoiding the allergen and using low-potency topical corticosteroids.
The inflammatory response can be blunted, so the rash may be less red and less blistering, and it may persist longer.

general.mild: Comfortable, alert, no distress; scratching occasionally
general.moderate: Mildly uncomfortable, visibly scratching, no systemic symptoms
general.severe: Distressed by intense itching, restless, may have sleep deprivation
general.critical: Not applicable; allergic contact dermatitis is not a critical illness

findings.maneuver: Inspect the affected skin in good lighting
findings.finding: Erythematous papules and vesicles confined to the area of contact

findings.maneuver: Inspect the pattern and borders of the rash
findings.finding: Linear or streaked distribution corresponding to how the allergen was brushed or spread across the skin

findings.maneuver: Inspect the borders of the rash
findings.finding: Sharply demarcated borders that stop abruptly at the edge of contact

findings.maneuver: Inspect the surface of the rash
findings.finding: Weeping, oozing and honey-colored or serous crusting
Localized swelling and induration of the involved skin

findings.maneuver: Inspect and palpate chronically affected skin
findings.finding: Thickened, leathery skin with exaggerated skin markings from chronic rubbing
Brown discoloration of skin where the rash has resolved

findings.maneuver: Measure temperature and assess for systemic signs
Inspect the oral, ocular and genital mucosae
findings.finding: No mucosal erosions, ulcers or conjunctival injection

findings.maneuver: Inspect the rash for pustules or purulent drainage

findings.finding: No pitting, ridging or nail dystrophy

labs.caveat: Peripheral eosinophilia is inconsistent and not required; a normal count does not argue against allergic contact dermatitis.
Usually normal; a marked rise should prompt reconsideration of infection or another systemic process.
Usually normal in uncomplicated allergic contact dermatitis.
Ordered to exclude a dermatophyte when the rash is annular, scaly or has an active border; a positive result points to tinea rather than allergic contact dermatitis.

The confirmatory test; results are read at 48 and 72–96 hours and must be interpreted with the exposure history. A positive result identifies sensitization, not necessarily the cause of the current rash.

findings.text: Allergic contact dermatitis is a clinical diagnosis; skin biopsy is rarely needed and imaging has no role.

initial.why: Identifies the responsible contact allergen when the cause is not obvious from the history and distribution.
Excludes tinea when the rash is annular, scaly or has a raised active border.
initial.only_if: the rash is annular or scaly and tinea is a consideration

supporting.why: Not routinely needed; may show mild eosinophilia and helps exclude infection when systemic signs are present.
supporting.only_if: systemic symptoms, extensive rash or concern for infection

supporting.why: Identifies bacterial superinfection when there is purulence, honey-colored crust or increasing pain.

not_indicated.why: Inflammatory markers are usually normal and are not part of the diagnosis.
Not useful in a localized contact dermatitis.
No role unless a viral vesicular eruption such as herpes simplex or varicella-zoster is being considered.
Reserved for atypical, persistent or diagnostically uncertain cases; histology is not specific.

decision_points: Diagnosis is clinical: exposure history plus a pruritic, sharply demarcated eczematous rash in the distribution of contact.
Patch testing is reserved for chronic, recurrent or occupationally significant cases, or when the allergen is unclear.
Consider KOH or fungal culture before patch testing when the rash is annular and scaly.
Reconsider the diagnosis if there is fever, mucosal involvement, purulence or spread to skin that never touched the allergen.

differential.name: Cellulitis
differential.why_considered: Red, swollen, warm skin with pain can look like an inflamed contact dermatitis, especially on the lower leg.
differential.trigger: Fever, spreading warmth, or a rash that is unilateral, tender and poorly demarcated

history: Fever and feeling unwell
Rapid progression over hours rather than days
No clear exposure to a contact allergen
Often a break in the skin, wound or prior episode
exam: Warm, tender, indurated skin with poorly defined borders
labs: Blood cultures positive in severe cases
imaging: Ultrasound or MRI only if abscess or deep infection is suspected

differential.name: Tinea (dermatophyte infection)
differential.why_considered: Annular, scaly, itchy rash with a raised border can mimic contact dermatitis, particularly on the hands and feet.

history: Slowly enlarging ring-shaped rash
Often no clear contact exposure
May have athlete's foot or nail involvement
exam: Annular plaque with an active, scaly, raised border and central clearing
Well-defined edge with scale, not vesicles
Nail thickening or discoloration if nails involved

differential.name: Atopic dermatitis
differential.why_considered: Chronic itchy, eczematous rash with dry skin and lichenification can resemble chronic contact dermatitis.

history: Personal or family history of atopy (asthma, allergic rhinitis, eczema)
Chronic, relapsing course since childhood
No clear relationship to a specific contactant
labs: No specific test; patch testing negative to suspected allergens

differential.name: Psoriasis
differential.why_considered: Well-demarcated erythematous plaques can be mistaken for contact dermatitis, especially on the hands.

history: Chronic, stable plaques
Family history of psoriasis
Often involves extensor surfaces, scalp, nails
exam: Auspitz sign (pinpoint bleeding when scale removed)
labs: No specific test; biopsy shows characteristic epidermal changes if needed

differential.name: Irritant contact dermatitis
differential.why_considered: Non-immune skin inflammation from direct chemical or physical irritation can look identical to allergic contact dermatitis.

history: Exposure to irritants such as soaps, detergents, solvents, acids or alkalis
Symptoms begin within minutes to hours of exposure
No prior sensitization required
Burning or stinging more prominent than itching
exam: Sharply demarcated erythema, dryness, fissures, or erosions
Less vesiculation than allergic contact dermatitis
Distribution matches the area of maximal exposure

differential.name: Sarcoidosis (cutaneous)
differential.why_considered: Cutaneous sarcoidosis can present with papules, plaques or nodules that may be mistaken for a contact dermatitis, especially on the face.

history: Systemic symptoms such as fever, weight loss, night sweats, cough, dyspnea
No clear contact exposure
Chronic, non-itchy lesions
exam: Firm, non-scaly papules or plaques, often violaceous or brownish-red
Lupus pernio (violaceous plaques on nose, cheeks, ears)
imaging: Chest X-ray showing hilar lymphadenopathy or interstitial changes

severity.mild: Localized area of erythema and mild itching, no vesicles, no functional impairment; resolves with avoidance and topical therapy.
severity.moderate: More extensive erythema with vesicles, oozing, and intense pruritus that interferes with sleep or daily activities; requires topical corticosteroids and possibly short course of systemic steroids.
severity.severe: Widespread involvement, marked edema, bullae, severe itching, or secondary infection; may require systemic corticosteroids and specialist referral.
severity.critical: Not applicable; allergic contact dermatitis is not a life-threatening condition.

red_flags.meaning: Suggests infection (cellulitis, bacteremia) rather than uncomplicated contact dermatitis.

red_flags.finding: Rapidly spreading erythema, warmth, tenderness, or purulent drainage
red_flags.meaning: Possible bacterial superinfection or cellulitis requiring antibiotics.

red_flags.finding: Mucosal involvement (oral, ocular, genital) or conjunctival injection
red_flags.meaning: Suggests a different diagnosis such as erythema multiforme, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, or another systemic dermatosis.

red_flags.finding: Rash involving skin that never contacted the allergen, or generalized eruption
red_flags.meaning: Consider systemic contact dermatitis, drug eruption, or other widespread dermatosis.

red_flags.finding: Severe swelling of the face, lips, or tongue, or difficulty breathing
red_flags.meaning: May indicate angioedema or anaphylaxis, which requires emergency evaluation.

complications.name: Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation
clues: Brown discoloration in areas of resolved rash
More prominent in darker skin types

complications.name: Lichenification
clues: Thickened, leathery skin with exaggerated markings
History of chronic rubbing or scratching

complications.name: Chronic dermatitis
clues: Persistent rash despite avoidance of suspected allergen

special_populations.differences: More often affects the face, hands, and diaper area; history of exposure may be unclear; irritability and scratching are common; management focuses on avoidance and low-potency topical corticosteroids.
Rash may be drier and less blistering; more often caused by topical medications or dressings; itching can be severe with minimal visible inflammation; higher risk of chronicity.
May be mistaken for a pregnancy-specific dermatosis; management focuses on allergen avoidance and low-potency topical corticosteroids; patch testing can be done if needed.
Inflammatory response may be blunted, so rash may be less red and less blistering; may persist longer and be more prone to secondary infection.

key_questions.question: What were you doing or touching right before the rash started — new soaps, lotions, jewelry, gloves, shoes, hair dye, or plants?
key_questions.looking_for: A specific contactant that matches the location and timing of the rash

key_questions.question: How long after that contact did the rash appear?
key_questions.looking_for: 24–72 hours in a previously sensitized person; up to 1–3 weeks after a first-ever exposure

key_questions.question: Where did the rash start, and has it spread?
key_questions.looking_for: Onset at the site of contact, with spread only to areas touched by contaminated hands or clothing

key_questions.question: Does it itch, burn or sting?
key_questions.looking_for: Intense itching; burning or stinging is more typical of an irritant reaction

key_questions.question: Did it start as red bumps and then blister or weep?
key_questions.looking_for: Papules and vesicles with oozing and crusting, the classic eczematous evolution

key_questions.question: Have you had this rash in the same spot before after similar contact?
key_questions.looking_for: Recurrence with re-exposure, supporting an acquired hypersensitivity

key_questions.question: What do you do for work, and what are your hobbies?
key_questions.looking_for: Occupational or recreational exposure to metals, rubber, cement, dyes, solvents or plants

key_questions.question: Do you have eczema, asthma or hay fever?
key_questions.looking_for: A personal or family history of atopy, which increases risk

key_questions.question: What creams, ointments, antibiotics or antihistamines have you put on your skin?
key_questions.looking_for: Topical products that can themselves be allergens, such as neomycin, bacitracin, benzocaine or diphenhydramine

key_questions.question: Do you wear jewelry, a watch, belt buckles or snaps that touch the rash?
key_questions.looking_for: Nickel-containing items, especially with ear piercing or a known metal allergy

key_questions.question: Any fever, feeling unwell, or rash in areas that never touched anything?
key_questions.looking_for: Systemic symptoms or generalized spread, which argue against uncomplicated contact dermatitis

key_questions.question: Any sores in your mouth, eyes or genitals?
key_questions.looking_for: Mucosal involvement suggesting erythema multiforme, Stevens-Johnson syndrome or another dermatosis

reasoning_points: A pruritic, eczematous rash confined to the skin that contacted the allergen, with sharply demarcated or linear borders
Onset 24–72 hours after re-exposure in a sensitized person, or up to 1–3 weeks after first-ever exposure
An identifiable contactant from the history — plants, nickel, fragrances, preservatives, topical antibiotics, rubber, hair dye or industrial chemicals
Papules and vesicles with oozing and crusting that may spread only to areas touched by contaminated hands or clothing
Absence of fever, systemic illness, mucosal involvement and purulence
Patch testing identifies the responsible allergen when the cause is not obvious and is read at 48 and 72–96 hours
KOH prep or fungal culture excludes tinea when the rash is annular and scaly
The diagnosis is clinical; biopsy and imaging are not needed in typical cases

easy: Clear exposure to poison ivy, oak or sumac with a linear, streaked vesicular rash
Rash confined to the earlobes, wrists or waistband under nickel-containing metal
Intense itching with vesicles and oozing in the distribution of contact
No fever, no mucosal involvement, no systemic symptoms
medium: Hand dermatitis in a hairdresser, healthcare worker or cleaner with mixed irritant and allergic exposures
Rash from a topical antibiotic or antihistamine applied to an initial dermatitis
Annular scaly rash that requires KOH testing to exclude tinea
Chronic, lichenified rash from ongoing unidentified exposure
hard: Older adult with a dry, minimally blistering rash from a dressing or topical medication
Immunocompromised patient with a blunted, less red and less vesicular eruption
Pregnant patient whose rash is mistaken for a pregnancy-specific dermatosis
Child with facial and diaper-area involvement and an unclear exposure history
Generalized or airborne eruption from burning vegetation, raising concern for a systemic process
